# Cinchona bark (quinine) against malaria (`quinine`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by malaria_mosquito, distillation, world_geography
- Core idea: Cinchona bark from Andean cloud forests contains quinine and related alkaloids that act on the blood stages of malaria parasites. Historically the dried bark was powdered and given for intermittent fevers. Bark from different trees varied greatly in strength, so a weight of bark could not specify the dose. Isolation of quinine made measured treatment possible. Ringing ears, nausea and hearing changes are adverse effects and cannot establish that treatment is adequate. Some malaria parasites have dormant liver stages that quinine does not clear.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting to find the tree in Europe, Asia or Africa before the 1850s; seeds had to be smuggled from South America
  - Using it for every fever; it does nothing for plague, typhus or typhoid
  - Confusing it with willow bark, which is bitter and lowers fever a little but does not cure malaria
  - Repeating the Countess of Chinchón story, a 17th-century legend; so is the idea that tonic water is a useful dose
  - Overdose: deafness, blindness, heart failure
- History: americas: c. 1630 – Jesuits in Peru (Lima, Loja) learn of the bark; whether Andean peoples used it against fever before the Spanish is uncertain, as malaria probably arrived with them; europe: 1640s – bark reaches Rome ('Jesuits' powder'); 1670s Talbor's secret remedy; 1712 Torti defines which fevers it cures; 1820 Pelletier and Caventou isolate quinine; china: c. 340 – Ge Hong recommends qinghao (Artemisia annua) soaked in cold water and wrung out for intermittent fevers; 1693 Jesuits cure the Kangxi emperor with cinchona; 1972 Tu Youyou's group isolates artemisinin; india: 1860s – British cinchona plantations (Nilgiris, Darjeeling) from Markham's seeds; east_asia: 1865 onward – Ledger's high-yield seeds grown by the Dutch in Java, which dominates world supply by 1900; africa: 1854 – Baikie's Niger expedition takes quinine daily and loses no one to fever
- Read:
  - Fiammetta Rocco, The Miraculous Fever-Tree: Malaria, Medicine and the Cure that Changed the World (2003)
  - Saul Jarcho, Quinine's Predecessor: Francesco Torti and the Early History of Cinchona (1993)
  - Youyou Tu, The discovery of artemisinin (qinghaosu) and gifts from Chinese medicine, Nature Medicine (2011)
